title: Are China’s Hospitals Less Profitable—or Is Profitability the Wrong Lens for Biomedical Innovation?
text:
Are China’s Hospitals Less Profitable—or Is Profitability the Wrong Lens for Biomedical Innovation?

Huiyan Li

August 20th, 2026

The NarrativeA common perception in China is that the U.S. hospitals leading the world in biomedical innovation are rich private institutions—and that their financial strength is a key reason they have been able to build the research capacity Chinese hospitals lack.In Chinese health-management research, analysis of these leading U.S. academic medical systems often highlights their strong asset positions and substantial investment returns. These financial resources support continued investment in innovation, and are often cited as a model for how Chinese research hospitals could build similar strength.The real obstacle, however, is not the balance sheet: it is whether China’s health system generates the flexible, long-term capital, talent, and institutions that biomedical innovation requires, and puts the country’s vast clinical scale to full use.Despite China’s rapid progress in life sciences, a substantial gap with the United States remains in clinical translation. The gap is particularly stark in investigator-initiated clinical research, where investigators take research questions from the laboratory into clinical studies.China ranks second globally in registered clinical trials, but this large volume has not translated into a comparable share of completed investigator-initiated trials with publicly reported results. Among the five countries with the most registered trials, China ranks last on this measure, at just 4%, compared with 54% in the United States.What Drives the NarrativeReports of local hospitals facing bankruptcies are frequent, and at the national level, public hospital debt in China nearly tripled over the past decade. Taken together, these trends paint a bleak picture of the financial health of China’s healthcare system.Based on headline financial terms,1 there is indeed a large revenue gap between Chinese and U.S. hospitals.West China Hospital of Sichuan University (四川大学华西医院), one of China’s leading academic medical hospitals and the country’s top recipient of National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) grants among medical institutions, generated roughly $1.75 billion in total revenue in FY2024. Mass General Brigham (MGB), an integrated academic health system that includes Massachusetts General Hospital, the largest recipient of NIH funding among U.S. independent hospitals, generated $21 billion in total revenue in FY2024, which was nearly 12 times West China’s total revenue.This gap is striking given that Chinese hospitals typically handle significantly higher patient volumes across outpatient visits, inpatient admissions, and surgical procedures. However, it is also worth noting that a large part of this disparity comes from differences in healthcare prices between the two countries.The Reality Check“The comparison of how much they earn misses the point; what matters is where the research money comes from, how talent is trained and retained, and how institutions are organized to connect them.”In reality, U.S. academic medical centers generate little profit from clinical care. According to Moody’s 2024 annual not-for-profit and public healthcare report, the median operating margin for U.S. hospitals was just 1.5% in 2024 (up from 0.5% in 2023), which means most hospitals operate with very thin margins on clinical services. MGB ran a $72 million operating loss in its core healthcare operations. Its roughly $2 billion net gain was driven almost entirely by investment portfolio returns and philanthropic donations, not patient care. By contrast, Chinese hospitals are almost entirely dependent on clinical revenue. This dependence can be traced back to the underfunding of public hospitals in the 1980s, when they were pushed to become financially self-sustaining.2 This created a system that rewards volume—more visits, more tests, more procedures—and, historically, a heavy reliance on drug sales. These incentives have proven difficult to change, even after subsequent reforms such as the elimination of drug markups and the introduction of a Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG) payment system designed to curb over-treatment by reimbursing hospitals a fixed amount per diagnosis rather than paying for each test, drug, and procedure.3The result, as a healthcare specialist puts it: “Every renminbi is squeezed from patient encounters.” PKU Professor Li Ling also notes: “Hospitals around the world generally do not make profits from clinical services—only Chinese hospitals do.”In other words, Chinese hospitals are already more dependent on clinical revenue than their American counterparts. Yet this very dependence on clinical revenue diverts resources and incentives away from research, constraining the development of sustained research capacity. A Narrower Funding BaseU.S. academic medical centers draw on multiple funding streams to support research, with major sources including external grants, investment returns, and philanthropic donations:Research grants constitute the most direct stream. In FY2025, MGB received about $3 billion in research grant income at the system level.Philanthropic donations add an important pillar. In FY2025, Mayo Clinic received $407 million in cash from donors. While not exclusively designated for research, donations provide flexible institutional capital. Investment portfolios at these institutions also generate returns that can be directed toward research and innovation. Together with donations, these returns provide hospitals with long-term, non-competitive capital not subject to project cycles or deliverable requirements.Chinese public hospitals’ research funding, by contrast, draws on a fundamentally narrower set of funding sources: competitive government grants (纵向科研经费), industry collaboration fees (横向科研经费), and direct hospital investment drawn from clinical revenue.The government grant channel is dominated by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), which disbursed approximately $4.4 billion in 2023 across all disciplines. Competition is fierce: in the medical sciences division, the funding rate for investigator-initiated grants (面上项目) stood at just 9.04% in 2024, the lowest of any NSFC panel. Moreover, NSFC provides only up to about $300,000 in funding per project, which is far from sufficient for medical research that requires extensive clinical studies and substantial financial investment. West China Hospital, the top hospital by number of NSFC grants, received 278 awards in 2025, totaling approximately $67 million in government research funding from the NSFC and other government bodies. By comparison, MGH received approximately $640.5 million in government research funding in FY2025—nearly ten times as much. At the system level, MGB received approximately $1.6 billion in government grants in FY2025.The industry collaboration channel is growing but remains local and focused on near-term application. Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital is located in one of China’s more developed biomedical industry hubs, with partners including leading firms such as Mindray and Taikang Insurance. It recorded 665 industry-funded projects totaling about $16 million from 2018 to 2023, averaging roughly $2.7 million annually. That this figure comes from one of China’s better-positioned hospitals underscores the limitations of industry collaboration as a research funding source.Direct hospital investment from clinical revenue is the third and structurally significant channel. West China Hospital discloses that it invests approximately $70 million to support innovation and translational research. This institutionally directed investment offers somewhat more flexibility than competitive project-based government grants. However, this funding is ultimately derived from clinical revenue and is therefore exposed to the same reimbursement pressures as broader hospital finances, including ongoing DRG reforms.

The Missing Physician-Scientist Physician-scientists account for just 1.3% of the U.S. physician workforce, yet they have played an important role in pioneering the translation of biomedical discoveries into clinical practice, including breakthroughs such as CAR-T cell therapy. Developing and retaining this workforce requires institutional support that enables physicians to pursue research careers, particularly during the early stages of their academic careers.In the United States, federal agencies, private foundations, and academic medical centers have established formal mechanisms to protect research time. NIH K awards require institutions to guarantee a minimum of 75% research time for funded physician-scientists. Private foundations such as Damon Runyon set the threshold at 80% throughout the award period. Academic medical centers also offer their own programs: Mayo Clinic’s multiple programs, for instance, provide up to 100% protected research time.In China, this infrastructure remains far less developed and institutionalized. Most hospitals prioritize patient volume over research, and protected research time remains largely unavailable. While the national performance evaluation system for tertiary public hospitals (三级公立医院绩效考核) does include two research-related indicators (research grants per 100 clinical staff and technology commercialization income), medical quality and operational efficiency remain the dominant dimensions of the framework among the 55 metrics. Research output carries only marginal institutional weight, driven more by promotion incentives than scientific pursuit, and may encourage repetitive, low-quality research. Physician compensation is also typically tied to hospital clinical revenue rather than research productivity.Medical education compounds the problem. China’s traditional five-year curriculum emphasizes clinical skills with limited research training. Progress is underway as 14 universities now offer eight-year integrated medical programs enrolling approximately 1,500 students annually, which combine clinical education with more substantial research training. However, integration between medical schools, affiliated hospitals, and research training remains uneven and incomplete.Even the U.S. side of this comparison is not without strain. A 2025 National Academy of Medicine workshop noted that physician-scientists now wait nearly a decade longer for their first major NIH research award than they did in the early 1980s, when most secured one in their early thirties. Even for funded physician-scientists, U.S. health systems are increasingly prioritizing clinical efficiency over research engagement, making it more difficult to sustain protected research time throughout their careers.A Fragmented Institutional ArchitectureThe funding and personnel constraints reflect a coordination failure at the system level: Chinese public hospitals conduct research, but no single institution is responsible for producing the integrated physician-scientist that translational medicine requires. Medical schools fall under the Ministry of Education; hospitals under the National Health Commission. Each optimizes for a different output function, with no coordinating mechanism to align them around clinical research training.By contrast, the U.S. academic health systems (AHS) are structurally integrated. Medical education, clinical care, and research operate under more integrated governance, with federal grants and institutional programs embedding protected research time into physician-scientist careers, shared endowments funding long-horizon inquiry, and technology transfer offices providing commercialization pathways.China’s most deliberate current attempt is Tsinghua Medicine, established in 2021 with an explicit mandate to integrate medical schools and affiliated hospitals into a functioning academic health system. As its founding dean has noted, the challenge is political—rooted in institutional disconnection—rather than technical.The Bottom LineThe point is not that Chinese hospitals are poorer than their American counterparts, or that they simply need more research funding. China already has extraordinary clinical scale and scientific talent. The deeper challenge is building the institutions needed to turn those advantages into sustained biomedical discovery.The strength of U.S. frontier biomedical research comes from diversified funding streams that support research independent of patient care revenue, together with institutional mechanisms that enable physician-scientists to pursue sustained research careers.Chinese hospitals, by contrast, are structurally dependent on clinical volume. The real constraints are a narrow and competitive funding base, the absence of a physician-scientist model, and a fragmented institutional architecture that produces neither the people nor the organizational conditions that translational medicine requires. With insurance payments tightening under DRG payment systems, where fixed per-case payments often fall short of actual treatment costs, especially for complex cases, many hospitals are struggling to meet basic payroll.Some regions have begun experimenting with incentive restructuring, most notably the Sanming model, which consolidates public health funds into a unified payment system tied to population health outcomes rather than service volume. But even this promising model faces significant headwinds: fiscal constraints at the local level, inter-agency coordination friction, and the internal disruption of redesigning physician performance metrics.At the same time, the U.S. system is not a model worth replicating wholesale: American healthcare is extraordinarily expensive, inequitable, and full of its own structural dysfunctions. The goal, then, should not be to make Chinese hospitals look more like American ones. It should be to build the financial, institutional, and talent infrastructure needed to connect China’s enormous clinical scale and talent pool with its growing biotech sector, which the government has identified as an emerging pillar industry. EndnotesChinese public hospitals and U.S. academic health systems differ substantially in organizational structure, scale, and financial reporting. West China Hospital is a single hospital, while MGB is a consolidated academic health system spanning multiple hospitals and other health care entities, including Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. The comparison is therefore intended to illustrate the broad difference in financial resources between leading research-oriented hospitals and health systems, rather than establish precise institutional equivalence.China’s post-1978 economic restructuring led to a sharp decline in state transfers to the health sector. As government revenue fell from roughly 30% to 10% of GDP between 1978 and 1993, subsidies to public hospitals dropped from 50–60% of their total revenues to approximately 10% by the early 1990s. With little deliberate policy attention directed at health care, public hospitals were left to finance themselves through patient charges, setting in motion the volume-driven incentive structure that persists today. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.4161/23288604.2014.995005#d1e198DRG is a payment system under which China’s national basic medical insurance, the country’s dominant payer, reimburses hospitals a fixed amount per case based on diagnosis, rather than reimbursing each service on a fee-for-service basis. The reform reduces incentives for unnecessary tests and procedures, but it has also created new financial pressures: fixed payments compress hospital revenue, while the underlying financing model remains unchanged. Chinese public hospitals continue to rely heavily on clinical revenue to cover their operating costs, leaving them with limited room to absorb rising costs or invest in research and other long-term capabilities when reimbursement falls short.
